summary: Describes IP fragmentation and explains why it makes Internet communication fragile. It proposes alternatives to fragmentation and gives recommendations to developers and network operators. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Chopping a large parcel into pieces to fit through a small door is risky, since if one piece is lost the whole parcel is useless. This document explains the risks and suggests better ways to send big things.

questions: why do icmp packet too big messages get lost
subtitle: Why splitting IP packets into fragments breaks so often on the real Internet, and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: When a packet is bigger than a path can carry, IP can split it into fragments. Many devices on the path handle fragments badly, so fragmented traffic is dropped, misrouted, abused by attackers or corrupted.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues the ways fragmentation fails (routing, NAT, firewalls, load balancing, ID collisions, attacks, lost ICMP messages), then describes alternatives such as keeping transport segments small and probing the path MTU.
tldr.outcome: It does not deprecate fragmentation, but tells developers not to build new protocols that depend on it and tells operators to keep PMTUD working.

today: RFC 8900 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 230, September 2020) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It deliberately stops short of deprecating IP fragmentation and instead tells new protocols to avoid relying on it.

sections.title: The Case Against Relying on Fragmentation
sections.content:
Operational experience shows that IP fragmentation makes Internet communication fragile. This RFC describes fragmentation, explains the fragility, proposes alternatives and gives recommendations to developers and network operators.

It does not recommend deprecating fragmentation. Some applications and environments still require it, and in those cases the designer should know that fragmented packets may be black-holed and should include safeguards. Instead, the RFC recommends that upper-layer protocols deal with the problem at their own layer and reduce their reliance on IP fragmentation as far as possible.
sections.eli5: Cutting a big parcel into pieces works, but it is risky. The advice is to pack smaller parcels in the first place.

sections.title: MTU, Path MTU and How Fragmentation Works
sections.content:
Each link has a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), the number of octets it can carry in one IP packet. IPv4 requires every link to support an MTU of 68 octets or greater, and IPv6 requires 1280 octets or greater. The Path MTU (PMTU) is the smallest link MTU along a path, and since paths change, so does the PMTU.

A source can be very conservative and assume the minimum link MTU, which is safe but may hurt performance. With Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD, RFC 1191 and RFC 8201), the source starts with the first link's MTU and sends non-fragmentable packets. A router that cannot forward one drops it and returns an ICMP Packet Too Big (PTB) message that carries the MTU of the link, which the source uses to refine its estimate. PMTUD fails if the network cannot deliver those messages, and because ICMP messages are easily forged and not authenticated, an attacker can force needlessly low estimates.

When the resulting packet exceeds the PMTU, it is divided into fragments, each with an IP header and part of the original. In IPv4, a packet with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set to 1 cannot be fragmented by a downstream router, while a packet with DF set to 0 can. In IPv6, only the source may fragment. In IPv6 the upper-layer header must be in the first fragment.

Upper-layer protocols can avoid fragmentation, rely on it at the source only, or (over IPv4 only) rely on it by any node. The first two need a PMTU estimate, which they can get from the minimum MTU, from PMTUD, or from Packetization Layer PMTUD (PLPMTUD, RFC 4821 and RFC 8899). PLPMTUD sends probe packets and relies on acknowledgements rather than on ICMP PTB messages.
sections.eli5: Every road has a narrowest spot. A truck that is too wide gets sent back with a note saying how wide the spot is. Sometimes the note gets lost.

sections.title: How Fragmentation Makes Things Fragile
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC lists the specific problems:

  • Virtual reassembly: devices such as Carrier Grade NAT must conceptually reassemble packets to translate fragments. This is computationally expensive and holds state for indeterminate periods, so it is prone to errors and attacks.
  • Policy-based routing: only the first fragment carries the transport header, so a later fragment can match a different forwarding entry and be sent to a different next hop.
  • NAT: the device must virtually reassemble packets to translate each fragment.
  • Stateless firewalls: port information is in the first fragment only, so the firewall must either accept all later fragments or block them all.
  • ECMP, LAG and load balancers: hashing uses a 5-tuple when a transport header is present but only a 3-tuple otherwise, so fragments of one flow can take different links.
  • IPv4 reassembly errors: at high data rates the 16-bit identification field cannot prevent duplicate IDs, and TCP and UDP checksums are insufficient to stop corrupted datagrams reaching upper layers. The IPv6 identification field is 32 bits.

Fragmentation is a stateful procedure inside a stateless protocol, which is why attackers can exploit it.
sections.eli5: Many helpers along the road only read the label on the first piece of a split parcel. The other pieces have no label, so the helpers do not know where they belong.

sections.title: Attacks and Black Holes
sections.content:
Documented attacks that exploit fragmentation include overlapping fragment attacks, resource exhaustion, attacks using predictable fragment identification values, and evasion of Network Intrusion Detection Systems. In an overlapping fragment attack, a first fragment passes the firewall, then a second overlapping fragment overwrites the transport header on reassembly so the result would have been rejected had it arrived whole. A stateless firewall cannot stop this, but destination nodes can by detecting the overlap and discarding the packet. In a resource exhaustion attack, packets are sent with a fragment missing so reassembly never completes and buffers stay occupied.

Fragmentation also causes PMTU black holes. PMTUD depends on ICMP PTB messages, which can be lost transiently (congestion, corruption, routing loops, rate limiting) or persistently. Persistent causes include incorrect security policy on consumer CPE routers that discard PTB messages, anycast (the message may reach a different instance of the same address), and unidirectional routing, where an intermediate node has no route back to the source. Black holes do not occur when the PMTU estimate comes from PLPMTUD.

Fragments themselves are often dropped. A study cited in RFC 7872 found that at least 28% of sampled paths did not convey packets with the IPv6 Fragment extension header, and another study reported that 37% of sampled endpoints used IPv6-capable DNS resolvers unable to receive a fragmented IPv6 response.
sections.eli5: Sneaky people can hand in pieces that overlap to trick the guard. And if the note saying the truck is too wide gets lost, the truck keeps getting turned away and never knows why.

sections.title: Alternatives to Fragmentation
sections.content:
Transport layer. TCP can run without IP fragmentation by keeping each segment under the Maximum Segment Size (MSS). The MSS can be set manually (always applicable, but it cannot take advantage of larger MTUs), by PMTUD (only where ICMP PTB loss is acceptable) or by PLPMTUD, which probes with TCP segments and does not reduce the congestion window when a probe is lost. DCCP and SCTP can also operate without IP fragmentation, and RFC 8899 gives PLPMTUD procedures for UDP, UDP options, SCTP, QUIC and other datagram protocols. UDP has no fragmentation mechanism of its own, so it relies on IP fragmentation, although a draft proposes one for UDP.

Application layer. RFC 8085 advises that an application SHOULD NOT send UDP datagrams that result in IP packets exceeding the path MTU, and should either use the PMTU information from the IP layer or implement PMTUD itself. Applications that do neither SHOULD still fall back to messages shorter than the default effective MTU for sending, which is the smaller of 576 bytes and the first-hop MTU for IPv4, and 1280 bytes for IPv6. The same advice applies to any application running directly over IP.
sections.eli5: The easy fix is to pack smaller boxes from the start, so nothing needs cutting, and to test the road with small trial boxes first.

sections.title: Applications That Still Rely on Fragmentation
sections.content:
Some applications rely on IPv6 fragmentation to varying degrees, sometimes essentially and sometimes incidentally. The list is not comprehensive.

  • DNS: it uses UDP for efficiency, so large responses may be fragmented. Smaller EDNS0 buffer sizes or a server-imposed maximum make large responses truncated so clients retry over TCP, but partial support for DNS over TCP limits this. DNSSEC's large keys make responses bigger and the RFC sees no effective answer within DNS except smaller keys and administrative practices that keep responses short.
  • OSPF: implementations can emit messages large enough to fragment, but most restrict message size to avoid it.
  • Packet-in-packet encapsulations (IP-in-IP, GRE, GRE-in-UDP, generic packet tunneling in IPv6): in some cases packets must be fragmented, so the RFC makes no extra recommendations for IP-in-IP tunnels.
  • UDP applications chasing performance: some use datagrams larger than the PMTU to move more data per system call. The RFC cites the Licklider Transmission Protocol, in current use on the International Space Station, and notes SNMP and video applications may do similar.
sections.eli5: Some old systems still need big parcels cut into pieces, like mail trains or space links, and that is allowed. Just do not build new ones that way.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC gives recommendations to each audience.

  • Application and protocol developers: SHOULD NOT develop new protocols or applications that rely on IP fragmentation, and they SHOULD work correctly in environments that do not fully support it. Legacy protocols SHOULD be updated to break the dependency, though sometimes there is no viable alternative (the RFC names IPsec tunnel mode and IP-in-IP). UDP applications SHOULD follow Section 3.2 of RFC 8085.
  • System developers: software libraries SHOULD include PLPMTUD for each supported transport protocol.
  • Middlebox developers: handle fragments consistently with RFC 791 and RFC 8200. Stateless behaviour that is non-compliant or discards fragments is NOT RECOMMENDED, and any nonstandard behaviour MUST be clearly documented.
  • ECMP, LAG and load-balancer developers and operators: when the IPv6 Flow Label is nonzero, devices SHOULD by default hash only the source address, destination address and Flow Label, and operators SHOULD keep that default.
  • Network operators: MUST ensure proper PMTUD operation, including generating PTB packets (rate limiting is allowed); MUST NOT filter ICMPv6 PTB messages unless known to be forged or illegitimate; MUST NOT deploy IPv6 links with an MTU under 1280 octets; and SHOULD NOT filter IP fragments from or to a domain name server.
sections.eli5: Builders should make smaller parcels. Road crews must keep the too-wide notes flowing. Guards must not throw away parcel pieces.
